theory.intro: Standard deviation only responds to changes that alter how far the data values sit from their **mean** — not to every change equally. Two changes come up again and again: **shifting every value by the same amount**, and **adding one new value** to the dataset.
facts: Adding (or subtracting) the same constant to **every** value shifts the **mean** by that constant, but leaves the **spread** of the data — and therefore $\sigma_x$ — **unchanged**.
This is true no matter how large or small the constant is.
Adding a **single new value equal to the current mean** pulls the average distance from the mean **down**, so $\sigma_x$ **decreases**.
Adding a **single new value far outside** the current data (an outlier) pulls the average distance from the mean **up**, so $\sigma_x$ **increases**.
If every value in a dataset is identical, there is no spread at all, so $\sigma_x = 0$.
steps: Identify what changes about the dataset
Decide the effect on the mean
Decide the effect on the standard deviation

foundation.question_text: A team's $5$ employees have a mean weekly wage of $\$620$ and population standard deviation $\$45$. Each employee is given a $\$30$ pay rise. State the new mean wage, and explain why the standard deviation is unchanged.
foundation.solution_text:
$\overline{x} = 620 + 30$
$= \$650$
Every wage shifted by the same $\$30$, so the spread between wages — and therefore $\sigma_x = \$45$ — has not changed.

foundation.question_text: A team's $6$ employees have a mean weekly wage of $\$580$ and population standard deviation $\$38$. Due to a cost-saving measure, every employee's wage is cut by $\$15$. State the new mean wage, and explain why the standard deviation is unchanged.
foundation.solution_text:
$\overline{x} = 580 - 15$
$= \$565$
Every wage shifted down by the same $\$15$, so the spread between wages — and therefore $\sigma_x = \$38$ — has not changed.

foundation.question_text: A gym class's $6$ members have a mean of $24$ push-ups and population standard deviation $3.2$ push-ups in a fitness test. In the retest, every member does $4$ more push-ups. State the new mean, and explain why the standard deviation is unchanged.
foundation.solution_text:
$\overline{x} = 24 + 4$
$= 28$
Every member's count shifted up by the same $4$ push-ups, so the spread between them — and therefore $\sigma_x = 3.2$ — has not changed.

foundation.question_text: Five employees have wages with mean $\$600$ and population standard deviation $\$50$. A new employee joins earning exactly $\$600$. Explain why adding this employee decreases the standard deviation.
foundation.solution_text:
The new employee's wage, $\$600$, is exactly at the mean, so its distance from the mean is $\$0$ — far less than the existing average distance of $\$50$.
Including this value pulls the average distance from the mean down, so $\sigma_x$ decreases.

foundation.question_text: Six gym members have a mean of $22$ push-ups and population standard deviation $2.8$ push-ups. A new member joins the class and manages only $4$ push-ups. Explain why adding this member increases the standard deviation.
foundation.solution_text:
The new member's count, $4$, is $18$ push-ups from the mean of $22$ — far more than the existing average distance of $2.8$ push-ups.
Including this far-below-average value pulls the average distance from the mean up, so $\sigma_x$ increases.

foundation.question_text: A manager currently pays $6$ staff different casual rates, with population standard deviation $\$62$. She proposes a flat rate: every staff member will be paid exactly the same rate, equal to the current mean rate. What will the new standard deviation be? Explain.
foundation.solution_text:
$\sigma_x = 0$
When every staff member is paid the same rate, there is no spread at all between the wages.

foundation.question_text: A payroll manager wonders: will giving every employee a $\$500$ pay rise change the standard deviation by more than giving every employee a $\$50$ pay rise? Explain your answer.
foundation.solution_text:
No — adding a constant to every value shifts the mean but never changes $\sigma_x$, no matter how large or small that constant is.
Both pay rises leave $\sigma_x$ exactly the same.

development.question_text: Six employees at a small business earn weekly wages of $\$520$, $\$610$, $\$480$, $\$700$, $\$550$ and $\$640$. Calculate the mean, correct to $1$ decimal place, and the population standard deviation, correct to $2$ decimal places, of these wages. Every employee is then given a $\$25$ pay rise. State the new mean, and explain why $\sigma_x$ is unchanged.
development.solution_text:
$\overline{x} = 583.3333...$
$\approx \$583.3$
$\sigma_x = 74.5356...$
$\approx \$74.54$
After the rise, the new mean is $583.3 + 25 = \$608.3$.
$\sigma_x$ stays $\$74.54$, since every wage shifted by the same amount and the spread between them has not changed.

development.question_text: In a fitness challenge, $5$ gym members complete $22$, $18$, $25$, $20$ and $24$ push-ups. Calculate the mean and the population standard deviation of this dataset, correct to $2$ decimal places. In the next round, a stricter rule costs every member $3$ push-ups from their count. State the new mean, and explain why $\sigma_x$ is unchanged.
development.solution_text:
$\overline{x} = 21.8$
$\sigma_x = 2.5612...$
$\approx 2.56$
After the penalty, the new mean is $21.8 - 3 = 18.8$.
$\sigma_x$ stays $2.56$, since every count shifted down by the same amount and the spread between them has not changed.

development.question_text: Five employees earn wages of $\$500$, $\$600$, $\$550$, $\$650$ and $\$700$. Calculate the mean and the population standard deviation of these wages, correct to $2$ decimal places. A new employee then joins, earning exactly $\$600$. Calculate the new population standard deviation, correct to $2$ decimal places, and explain why it is smaller than before.
development.solution_text:
$\overline{x} = \$600$
$\sigma_x = 70.7107...$
$\approx \$70.71$
The new employee's wage, $\$600$, is exactly at the mean, so its distance from the mean is $\$0$ — much less than the original average distance of $\$70.71$.
$\sigma_x = 64.5497...$
$\approx \$64.55$
Including this value pulls the average distance from the mean down, so $\sigma_x$ decreases.

development.question_text: Five gym members complete $20$, $17$, $23$, $19$ and $21$ push-ups. Calculate the mean and the population standard deviation of this dataset, correct to $2$ decimal places. A new member then joins and manages only $2$ push-ups. Calculate the new population standard deviation, correct to $2$ decimal places, and explain why it is larger than before.
development.solution_text:
$\overline{x} = 20$
$\sigma_x = 2.0000...$
$\approx 2.00$
The new member's count, $2$, is $18$ push-ups from the original mean of $20$ — much further than the original spread of $2.00$.
$\sigma_x = 6.9522...$
$\approx 6.95$
Including this far-below-average value pulls the average distance from the mean up, so $\sigma_x$ increases.

development.question_text:
A payroll analyst is considering four possible changes to a company's wage dataset, which currently has mean $\$610$ and $\sigma_x = \$52$.
(i) Every wage increases by $\$40$.
(ii) A new employee joins earning $\$610$.
(iii) A new employee joins earning $\$1450$.
(iv) Every wage decreases by $\$25$.
For each change, state whether $\sigma_x$ increases, decreases, or stays the same.
development.solution_text:
(i) Adding the same amount to every wage does not change the spread, so $\sigma_x$ stays the same.
(ii) The new wage equals the current mean, so it pulls the average distance from the mean down: $\sigma_x$ decreases.
(iii) The new wage is far above every existing wage, so it pulls the average distance from the mean up: $\sigma_x$ increases.
(iv) Subtracting the same amount from every wage does not change the spread, so $\sigma_x$ stays the same.

development.question_text:
A gym's fitness-test results have a mean of $24$ push-ups and $\sigma_x = 3.5$ push-ups. Two changes are proposed.
(i) Every member does $3$ more push-ups in the retest.
(ii) A new member joins who can do exactly $24$ push-ups.
For each change, state the effect on both the mean and the standard deviation.
development.solution_text:
(i) Every count shifts up by $3$, so the mean increases to $27$, but the spread between counts is unchanged, so $\sigma_x$ stays $3.5$.
(ii) The new count, $24$, equals the current mean, so the mean barely moves, but this value is closer to the mean than the existing spread, so $\sigma_x$ decreases.

mastery.question_text: A company's six senior staff earn weekly wages of $\$500$, $\$540$, $\$580$, $\$620$, $\$660$ and $\$700$. Calculate the population standard deviation of these wages, correct to $2$ decimal places. The company then hires two new staff at once: one earning exactly $\$600$ (the original mean) and one very senior hire earning $\$1400$. Determine whether the overall standard deviation increases, decreases or stays about the same once both new wages are included, and justify your answer by comparing the size of each new wage's effect.
mastery.solution_text:
$\sigma_x = 68.3130...$
$\approx \$68.31$
The $\$600$ wage sits exactly at the original mean, so on its own it would pull $\sigma_x$ down.
The $\$1400$ wage is far more extreme than any existing wage, so on its own it would pull $\sigma_x$ up by a much larger amount.
$\sigma_x = 271.1088...$
$\approx \$271.11$
The far outlier's effect dominates the at-mean addition's effect, so the overall standard deviation increases sharply.

mastery.question_text: In a fitness challenge, $5$ gym members complete $40$, $45$, $50$, $55$ and $60$ push-ups. Calculate the mean and the population standard deviation of this dataset, correct to $2$ decimal places. Two more members then join: one who managed only $20$ push-ups and one who managed $80$ push-ups — the same distance below and above the original mean. Explain why the mean of all seven results is unchanged, but the standard deviation is not.
mastery.solution_text:
$\overline{x} = 50$
$\sigma_x = 7.0711...$
$\approx 7.07$
The two new values, $20$ and $80$, are the same distance ($30$) below and above the mean of $50$, so they balance out and leave the mean unchanged at $50$.
$\sigma_x = 17.1131...$
$\approx 17.11$
Both new values sit much further from the mean than the original spread of $7.07$, so they still increase the average distance from the mean — the mean staying the same does not mean the standard deviation stays the same.

mastery.question_text:
A gym's $5$ members complete a push-up test: $24$, $20$, $27$, $22$ and $26$ push-ups. Calculate the population standard deviation of this dataset, correct to $2$ decimal places.
In the retest, every member does $2$ more push-ups than before. State the new standard deviation without recalculating from scratch, and explain your reasoning.
A new member then joins the retest group, completing only $5$ push-ups. Find the new mean, correct to $1$ decimal place, and the new standard deviation, correct to $2$ decimal places, once this score is included, and describe how the standard deviation has changed since the very first calculation.
mastery.solution_text:
$\sigma_x = 2.5612...$
$\approx 2.56$
Every member's count shifts up by the same $2$ push-ups, so the spread is unchanged: $\sigma_x$ stays $2.56$.
Adding the new member's score of $5$ push-ups gives:
$\overline{x} = 22.3333...$
$\approx 22.3$
$\sigma_x = 8.0966...$
$\approx 8.10$
The $5$ push-up score is far below the group, so the standard deviation has risen sharply from the original $2.56$ to $8.10$.
